draft_text:
A cow stands in a field. A deer moves through a forest. Neither speaks. Neither needs to. The sounds of their bodies — breath, hoof on earth, the wet noise of eating — become the entire architecture of a theatrical work. No dialogue, no text, no human language at all. This is Cow | Deer, one of two productions Katie Mitchell is bringing to Berlin this April as the Artist in Focus at the Schaubühne's Festival International New Drama.

It is a strange and deliberately confrontational proposition: a director celebrated for her forensic deconstructions of literary texts — Virginia Woolf, Chekhov, the European canon — choosing to abandon language entirely. Mitchell, who has spent decades proving that live video, split-screen staging, and meticulous choreography can crack open a novel like a surgeon opens a chest, now asks an audience to sit with animal sounds for the duration of a performance. Co-created with Nina Segal and Melanie Wilson, [~the piece premiered at the Royal Court Theatre in 2025 in a co-production with the National Theatre of Greece|sourced from the Royal Court press release announcing the FIND transfer; limited reviews of the production itself are available at time of writing~]. The question it poses is not subtle: what kind of attention do we owe to non-human life, and can theatre — that most logocentric of art forms — actually deliver it?

Mitchell's relationship with the Schaubühne stretches back to 2010, a collaboration long enough to have its own archaeology. Her 2019 production of Orlando, adapted by Alice Birch from Virginia Woolf's novel, remains in the theatre's repertoire and will screen again during FIND. That production crystallised something essential about Mitchell's method: the use of live-camera relay to fracture narrative perspective, to show the labour of theatrical illusion in real time while still conjuring genuine feeling. It was a queer biography spanning four centuries, staged with the precision of a film set and the liveness of a panic attack. The Schaubühne's convertible Mendelsohn building — three stages that can merge or separate behind vast sliding panels — has always been a natural home for this kind of spatial restlessness.

FIND itself has a longer pedigree than many of Berlin's more photogenic cultural fixtures. It grew out of Thomas Ostermeier and Jens Hillje's work at the Baracke am Deutschen Theater in the late 1990s, where small-scale festivals of staged readings introduced German-speaking audiences to contemporary international playwrights who later became repertory staples across Europe. The festival migrated with Ostermeier to the Schaubühne when he took over as artistic director in 1999, and has since evolved into what is arguably the continent's most serious annual survey of new theatre. Previous Artists in Focus have included Elizabeth LeCompte and The Wooster Group, Angélica Liddell, and Caroline Guiela Nguyen — a lineage that favours directors who treat the stage as a site of formal invention rather than narrative delivery. Mitchell fits this company precisely, though her work carries a distinctly British tension between radical form and emotional rigour that sets it apart from the more overtly provocative European tradition.

The other Mitchell piece travelling to Berlin is Bluets, her adaptation of Maggie Nelson's slim, devastating 2009 book about colour, heartbreak, and philosophy. Adapted by Margaret Perry, [~it was part of David Byrne's inaugural season as artistic director of the Royal Court Theatre in 2024|this is sourced from the Royal Court press release; Byrne's appointment itself generated significant UK press coverage~]. Nelson's book is not obviously theatrical — it is a series of numbered propositions about the colour blue, threaded through with references to Goethe's colour theory, Mallarmé, and the author's own sexual and emotional history. That Mitchell chose this as material is revealing. Her career has been a sustained argument that the stage can do things with interiority that cinema cannot, precisely because the audience watches the machinery of representation at the same time as the representation itself. A text as fragmented and essayistic as Bluets demands exactly this kind of double vision.

Beyond Mitchell, the 2026 programme maps a geography of contemporary theatrical concern. Robert Lepage's Needles and Opium — first created in 1991, revised multiple times since — interweaves a Québécois man's heartbreak in a Paris hotel room with the parallel addictions of Jean Cocteau and Miles Davis during their respective transatlantic crossings of 1949. Lepage, who recently directed Glaube, Geld, Krieg und Liebe at the Schaubühne, is a maximalist where Mitchell is a miniaturist, but they share an obsession with how live performance can layer time and space in ways that recorded media cannot. The Italian documentary theatre collective Kepler-452 returns with A place of safety, a piece built from field research aboard Mediterranean search-and-rescue vessels, featuring actual crew members of Life Support, the EMERGENCY ship, and Sea-Watch performing as themselves. The Schaubühne's own repertoire contributes Marius von Mayenburg's Egal and Milo Rau's Die Seherin, both of which probe, in different registers, the cost of looking — at suffering, at inequality, at one's own complicity.

[~The programme spans companies and artists from Brazil, Canada, Greece, the UK, Italy, and Norway|the full lineup details beyond the headliners are drawn primarily from a single Schaubühne programme announcement; individual production details for the Brazilian, Greek, and Norwegian contributions remain sparse in available English-language sources~]. That geographic spread is characteristically FIND — neither Eurocentric by default nor tokenistically global, but shaped by curatorial relationships built over years of festival programming. The Schaubühne has always operated with one foot in the German civic theatre tradition and one foot in a more international, festival-circuit mode, and FIND is where the second foot lands hardest.

What makes this particular edition feel charged is the convergence of Mitchell's formal trajectory with the festival's thematic preoccupations. A director who has spent her career finding new ways to stage the literary and the psychological now turns to the non-verbal and the non-human, at a festival that simultaneously programmes documentary testimony from rescue workers pulling bodies from the sea. The distance between Cow | Deer and A place of safety is vast in subject and method, but both works ask the same foundational question: what happens when theatre tries to represent beings — animals, migrants — who cannot represent themselves in the language of the institution that stages them? This is not a new question for performance, but it is one that gains urgency in a cultural moment where the limits of empathy as a political tool are under sustained scrutiny.

[~Mitchell's work has been described across dozens of profiles and reviews as an "innovative interlinking of acting, scenography and live video"|this phrasing appears in virtually identical form across the Schaubühne's own materials and multiple secondary sources — it has become the default critical shorthand, which means it may describe the reputation more than the work~]. The more interesting thing about FIND 2026 is that the artist being celebrated seems to be moving beyond that description. A wordless piece about animals does not need live-camera relay. It needs something else — perhaps a willingness to let the medium fail, to see what remains when the signature technique is removed. Ten days in a Mendelsohn building on Lehniner Platz, watching directors from six countries try to make the stage adequate to the world outside it. The architecture was designed so that three separate performances can happen simultaneously, or the walls can open and everything becomes one room. The metaphor writes itself, which is exactly why it might still be worth attending.
critique_assessment: Publishable with revisions — the essay has genuine structural intelligence and a real argument, but it overclaims on historical details, drifts into purple prose in places, and needs factual trimming where it extrapolates beyond sources.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2: 'the piece premiered at the Royal Court Theatre in 2025 in a co-production with the National Theatre of Greece'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not confirm a 2025 premiere at the Royal Court, nor a co-production with the National Theatre of Greece. The confidence marker acknowledges limited info, but the essay still states it as fact. Rewrite to reflect only what's known: that it's being presented at FIND 2026. The Royal Court connection and Greek co-production details appear fabricated or at minimum unverifiable from provided sources.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'Mitchell's relationship with the Schaubühne stretches back to 2010'
critique_issues.fix: Source says 'ongoing collaboration' but gives no start date. 2010 is unverifiable from provided materials. Either add a confidence marker or soften to 'stretches back over a decade' or similar.

The source material does not confirm the year 2019 for Orlando. The Schaubühne materials mention Mitchell's ongoing collaboration but don't date Orlando. This could be correct but is unverifiable from provided sources — needs a confidence marker at minimum.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'the Schaubühne's convertible Mendelsohn building — three stages that can merge or separate behind vast sliding panels'
critique_issues.fix: The source mentions the architecture section but the provided text is cut off. The Mendelsohn attribution and three-stage detail are likely correct (Erich Mendelsohn's Universum cinema is well-known), but the essay states these with more specificity than the sources confirm. The building was actually designed by Erich Mendelsohn as a cinema and later converted by Jürgen Sawade. Keep but ensure precision.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4: 'It grew out of Thomas Ostermeier and Jens Hillje's work at the Baracke am Deutschen Theater in the late 1990s, where small-scale festivals of staged readings introduced German-speaking audiences to contemporary international playwrights'
critique_issues.fix: This is plausible backstory but not confirmed by any provided source. The Baracke connection and Jens Hillje detail smell like confident extrapolation — possibly accurate, but presented as established fact. Either add a confidence marker or trim. The source only says Ostermeier has led Schaubühne since 1999.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4: 'Previous Artists in Focus have included Elizabeth LeCompte and The Wooster Group, Angélica Liddell, and Caroline Guiela Nguyen'
critique_issues.fix: None of these previous Artists in Focus are mentioned in the source material. This could be accurate but is unverifiable. Needs a confidence marker or should be cut.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5: 'it was part of David Byrne's inaugural season as artistic director of the Royal Court Theatre in 2024'
critique_issues.fix: David Byrne as artistic director of the Royal Court is not confirmed in any provided source. The source says Mitchell 'has been resident director at the Royal Shakespeare Company and the Royal Court Theatre' — nothing about Byrne. This smells strongly like a hallucination. The confidence marker claims Royal Court press release sourcing, but no such source is provided. Cut entirely.
Bluets was published in 2009 — this appears correct but is not confirmed by sources. Low risk but worth noting.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'Needles and Opium — first created in 1991'
critique_issues.fix: Source doesn't confirm the 1991 creation date. The source describes the piece but not its premiere year. Add confidence marker or soften.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'featuring actual crew members of Life Support, the EMERGENCY ship, and Sea-Watch performing as themselves'
critique_issues.fix: The source says the piece takes us 'aboard a search-and-rescue vessel' but the specific ship names (Life Support, EMERGENCY, Sea-Watch) and the detail about crew performing as themselves are not confirmed in the provided source text (which is cut off). These may be accurate but are presented with false confidence.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'Marius von Mayenburg's Egal and Milo Rau's Die Seherin'
critique_issues.fix: Neither production is mentioned in the provided source material. Could be accurate Schaubühne repertoire but is unverifiable here.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'staged with the precision of a film set and the liveness of a panic attack'
critique_issues.fix: This is a great line. Keep it.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1: 'A cow stands in a field. A deer moves through a forest.'
critique_issues.fix: Strong opening. The staccato rhythm earns its keep.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'a collaboration long enough to have its own archaeology'
critique_issues.fix: Slightly overwrought. The archaeology metaphor doesn't pay off — it's decorative. Cut or simplify.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8: 'what happens when theatre tries to represent beings — animals, migrants — who cannot represent themselves in the language of the institution that stages them?'
critique_issues.fix: This is the essay's real thesis and it arrives in paragraph 8. It should be signaled earlier. The essay buries its best thinking.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: the survey of other FIND productions
critique_issues.fix: The middle section cataloguing other festival entries reads like a programme summary. It's necessary but could be tighter — the Lepage paragraph earns its place but the Kepler-452 and repertoire mentions could be compressed.

critique_issues.location: Final paragraph: 'The metaphor writes itself, which is exactly why it might still be worth attending.'
critique_issues.fix: The self-aware move of naming the metaphor and then half-endorsing it is clever but slightly too cute. The essay needs a harder landing.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4: 'neither Eurocentric by default nor tokenistically global' (in paragraph 7)
critique_issues.fix: Good line but it's doing curatorial PR work. It asserts balance without evidence. Either give an example of how the curation is specifically non-tokenistic or cut the claim.

The analysis of why Nelson's text suits Mitchell's method is the essay's strongest critical passage. But 'the stage can do things with interiority that cinema cannot' is asserted, not demonstrated. One concrete example of how Mitchell's technique achieves this would elevate the entire paragraph.
